title: I’m a 3D artist experimenting with AI to turn my character sketches into game assets
author: adrien_flex
selftext:
I’m a 3D artist working on my indie game, Ashenmoor. I’ve been using AI to get my ideas into a playable prototype quickly.

Here’s an example with this golem: I painted a quick concept in Krita, used AI to refine the image, made a few manual touch-ups, then generated the 3D model. I rigged and animated it in Blender before bringing it into Godot.

What I like about this process is how quickly I can see a character from one of my own drawings come to life in the game. I can try out my ideas together, then keep refining each asset as I go.

replies.author: call_stacks
replies.body: Just wondering did you rig and animate in blender by hand? I'm working on a concept game right now and I found this to be such a tedious and long time sink, granted I'm completely new to art/blender/rigging and animation - any resources you can suggest to upskill myself in that area?

replies.author: Curious-Birthday-609
replies.body: Auto rig pro. Inside blender. It’s paid. Otherwise mixamo (web) both for rigging. ARP will produce better results out of the gate and will allow you to have control rig inside blender. But mixamo is a fantastic free option and comes with the ease of adding mocap from their library. There’s also AccuRIG (free) by character creator. Cheers!

replies.author: call_stacks
replies.body: Thx was hoping for free approaches :) I suppose auto rig pro also works on non humanoid characters?

replies.author: Curious-Birthday-609
replies.body: 2nd two are free. ARP works on non humanoid but the ai auto rig only works on biped and makes it super fast. But manually placing the non humanoid isn’t hard, and will still auto weight

replies.author: adrien_flex
replies.body: Yes, I rigged and animated this in Blender. I use Rigify, and [GameRig](https://github.com/Arminando/GameRig) is worth a look if you need rigs that are easier to export to a game engine. For the cape, I just animated a chain of bones.

I’m trying to do a similar thing, but in Unreal.  
I’m having troubles at exporting or importing to UE. The animated and rigged character just looks deformed. Even damn pro plan on Claude can’t figure out what’s wrong. Maybe I’m missing some checkbox on export from Blender and import to UE? 

I know it’s a long shot, but maybe you could suggest what’s wrong? What’s the export pipeline you do? An FBX?

replies.author: adrien_flex
replies.body: I use Godot, so I can’t pinpoint the Unreal issue. If you’re using Rigify, have a look at [GameRig](https://github.com/Arminando/GameRig). Standard Rigify rigs aren’t always ideal for game-engine export. I can’t promise it will fix your deformation, but the rig itself is worth checking.

comments.author: Expensive-Tomato-311
comments.body:
I couldn't agree more  with this. In fact i believe AI's limits in game dev can be pushed even further.

For me, one of the interesting problems is environment creation. You can spend a huge amount of time creating assets and then even more time putting them together into something that actually feels like a coherent world.

I'm currently experimenting with a project called Forge that explores whether AI could generate small, explorable 3D environments from a natural-language description rather than just generating individual assets.

But before I go too far with it, I'd really like to hear from actual solo developers:

What's the part of game development that eats the most time for you?

And if you could automate one part of your workflow without losing creative control, what would it be?
